Discovered, Not Designed:
Population Evolution for Collaborative
and Compute-Intensive Model Discovery

Bo Peng Affiliation: Meta Equal contribution    Lizhu Zhang Affiliation: Meta Equal contribution    Yuhang Zhou Affiliation: Meta    Mingyi Wang Affiliation: Meta    Yifan Wu Affiliation: Meta    Serena Li Affiliation: Meta    Xiangjun Fan Affiliation: Meta    Zhuokai Zhao Affiliation: Meta
Abstract

LLM-driven evolution enables iterative model development, but two practical goals remain underexplored: finding model designs that transfer across related tasks and sustaining improvement when training is expensive. We introduce Population Evolution (PE), a collaborative, hierarchical framework that connects ongoing local searches through shared experimental evidence. PE evaluates code changes across related training instances and shares the results to guide subsequent proposals and promotion to larger training scales. For expensive targets, PE searches small training subsets and screens candidates through peer and intermediate evaluations before full-target training. We introduce RMD-Bench to evaluate both settings across ranking, watch-time prediction, RL algorithm discovery, and LLM/VLM pretraining. Compared with standalone evolution at matched source iterations, PE raises mean best local gains from 7.01% to 8.97% in ranking and from 2.84% to 3.85% in watch-time, while improving the best larger-scale outcome in all three joint-discovery families. In watch-time discovery, PE improves best larger-scale gains with four of five harnesses and all four proposers. On new recommendation datasets under shared target-side calibration, every evaluated PE design improves over the reference in mean performance. Under matched total GPU compute, completed LLM discovery runs yield a best relative accuracy gain of 2.48% and 13 successful candidates for PE, versus 0.92% and none for direct evolution. VLM loss reduction reaches 8.78% versus 5.05% under matched total GPU compute.

1 Introduction

LLM-driven evolution automates model development by proposing code changes, evaluating them, and using the results to guide further edits (Liu et al., 2024; Novikov et al., 2025; Lange et al., 2025). Related research agents automate idea generation and experimentation (Lu et al., 2024), while neural architecture discovery offers a route toward recursive self-improvement (Pepe et al., 2026). Despite this progress, two goals remain underexplored in LLM-driven neural model discovery: discovering universal model designs across related tasks and sustaining improvement when candidate training is expensive.

Collaborative model discovery within a domain. Related datasets often share modeling requirements, so a mechanism discovered on one can inform development on another. Independent single-task searches primarily use their own feedback (Novikov et al., 2025; Lange et al., 2025), leaving this evidence isolated. Connecting these searches can support both local improvement and universal model designs: a common architecture or training mechanism used across related instances, with parameters trained separately on each.

Sustaining discovery on computationally demanding tasks. When every candidate requires substantial computation, as in full LLM or VLM training, a fixed budget permits few proposal–evaluation cycles. Parallel full-target searches broaden exploration, but costly evaluations limit how many revisions each search can make (Novikov et al., 2025). Sustained discovery therefore requires affordable experiments that inform continued development, followed by verification under full-target training.

We introduce Population Evolution (PE), which connects ongoing local searches through a shared ledger of executable interventions and cross-instance evaluation results (Figure 1).

Each source retains its objective and archive; shared feedback guides local edits, while replay lets other instances reuse its discoveries. Cross-instance replay tests the same intervention after retraining under each receiving instance’s protocol.

In joint discovery, searches on related datasets or training configurations reuse, adapt, and combine mechanisms; replay and larger-scale evaluation establish where the resulting designs remain useful. In decomposed discovery, small subsets of an expensive target’s training data provide affordable search instances, with peer and intermediate evaluations directing candidates toward full-target training. This hierarchy supports iterative refinement while reserving full-target training for screened candidates.

We introduce the Recursive Model Discovery Benchmark (RMD-Bench), providing executable evaluation protocols for five task families spanning both settings. Compatible interfaces and fixed references support evaluation of local gains and transfer in joint discovery, and full-target quality and yield in decomposed discovery. All three joint-discovery families also test transfer to new datasets or disjoint coding tasks. We start from FuXi-Linear (Ye et al., 2026) for ranking, EGMN (Zhao et al., 2025) for watch-time prediction, GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) for RL algorithm discovery, Gemma 3-style architectures (Gemma Team, 2025) for LLM pretraining, and Qwen3.5-style architectures (Qwen Team, 2026) for VLM pretraining. A complete LLM or VLM discovery run, including five searches and their evaluations, requires thousands of GPU-hours.

At matched source iterations, PE improves the mean per-source best gain in both recommendation families and the best larger-scale outcome in all three joint-discovery families. Every evaluated PE recommendation design improves over the reference mean on new datasets. Retraining uses shared target-side calibration without candidate-specific tuning. For LLM pretraining, completed runs under matched total GPU compute yield a 2.48% best relative accuracy gain and 13 successful candidates for PE, versus 0.92% and none for direct evolution. For VLM pretraining, best loss reduction rises from 5.05% to 8.78% under matched total GPU compute. Our contributions are:

  • •

    Population Evolution: a collaborative and hierarchical framework that uses shared experimental feedback to guide local search, reuses executable interventions across instances, and promotes candidates across training scales.

  • •

    RMD-Bench: five executable task families with compatible code interfaces, shared reference implementations, and controlled cross-instance and cross-scale evaluation, including transfer to new datasets and tasks in all three Track A families.

  • •

    Model discoveries and transfer: recommendation designs that improve over shared references on new datasets, better larger-scale outcomes in all three Track A families, and successful full-target LLM/VLM interventions, with watch-time comparisons across harnesses and proposers.

2 Population Evolution

An instance EiE_{i} specifies the data, objective, and training/evaluation protocol. In standard single-task evolution, an LLM repeatedly edits model or training code on one instance, using evaluation feedback to guide subsequent proposals (Liu et al., 2024; Novikov et al., 2025); we call this a local search. PE connects local searches across related source instances 𝒟={Ei}\mathcal{D}=\{E_{i}\}, sharing evidence to guide proposals and promotion to larger training scales. A candidate is an executable intervention in model architecture or training code. A shared ledger MtM_{t} stores candidate records and evaluation results. Figure 1 summarizes local search, cross-instance sharing, and promotion; Algorithm 1 in Appendix B.4 gives the asynchronous loop.

2.1 Local search on each source instance

Each local search selects a parent from its own code archive. An LLM edits that parent’s model or training code, and the resulting candidate is trained and evaluated on the same source instance. Evaluation updates the local history and archive; PE supplements this feedback with shared experimental evidence. At proposal step tt, proposer pip_{i} generates candidate hi,th_{i,t} from local history τi,t\tau_{i,t} and shared evidence Φi​(Mt)\Phi_{i}(M_{t}):

hi,t∼pi​(h∣τi,t,Φi​(Mt)).h_{i,t}\sim p_{i}\!\left(h\mid\tau_{i,t},\Phi_{i}(M_{t})\right). (1)

With the local harness, proposer, and archive-update rules fixed, omitting Φi​(Mt)\Phi_{i}(M_{t}) reduces the source-search procedure to standalone evolution. Candidate code is inherited and edited; model parameters are trained separately for each evaluation.

2.2 Sharing and evaluating candidates across instances

When a candidate meets its source’s configured improvement criteria, PE publishes its executable intervention, mechanism description, provenance, and score to the shared ledger. The other source instances are its peers. PE restores each peer’s reference code, applies the published intervention, then trains and evaluates it under that peer’s protocol. We call this cross-instance replay (Figure 1(a)). All peer results, including weak or unsuccessful transfers, are added to the ledger.

Before every LLM call, Φi​(Mt)\Phi_{i}(M_{t}) summarizes the instance’s own published candidates and peer transfers to EiE_{i}, including mechanisms and measured outcomes of successful and unsuccessful transfers. Peer and promotion results affect local proposals only through this context; code archives remain instance-specific. The proposer can use these outcomes to reuse, modify, or combine mechanisms. Appendices B.2 and B.3 detail the shared records, proposal context, and prompt structure.

2.3 Promoting candidates to larger training scales

Shared results also govern promotion: published candidates must meet the configured improvement criteria on at least two of their four peers in our experiments (Appendix B.1).

In joint discovery (Track A), eligible candidates are retrained on a larger-scale instance. Peer and larger-scale results return to the ledger, supporting local improvement and identifying designs useful across related instances (Figure 1(b)).

In decomposed discovery (Track B), source searches run on affordable training subsets. Eligible candidates are tested on two intermediate instances; those passing both advance to full-target training (Figure 1(c)). Peer and intermediate results inform further proposals, while full-target scores and pass/fail outcomes are withheld from proposal context. This is intended to prevent a few full-target successes from prematurely steering all source searches toward similar designs. A candidate graduates when it passes the final stage: larger-scale evaluation in Track A or full-target evaluation in Track B. Local searches continue while these evaluations run asynchronously.

3 RMD-Bench: Tasks and Evaluation

RMD-Bench defines five task families with objectives, reference implementations, editable components, and executable training/evaluation protocols. Compatible interfaces support retraining across related instances. The 34 core instances vary data, training seed, or scale; Track A also evaluates transfer beyond discovery instances. The benchmark fixes evaluation conditions within each instance; each discovery system chooses its search, sharing, and selection policies. Table 1 compares benchmark support for these settings; Section 6 discusses related work, and Appendix A gives task specifications.

3.1 Joint discovery (Track A)

Track A tests local improvement and discovery of universal model designs useful across related tasks.

Discovery instances. Ranking, watch-time prediction, and RL algorithm discovery each have five source instances and one larger-scale instance (18 instances in total; Figure 1(b)). Within each recommendation family, the five sources use different datasets; watch-time includes CIKM16 and WeChat. Both families use KuaiRand-27K for larger-scale evaluation. Ranking edits sequence representations and temporal interactions in FuXi-Linear (Ye et al., 2026), using the mean of NDCG@10, HR@10, and MRR as its score. Watch-time discovery edits EGMN’s distributional head and point-prediction rule (Zhao et al., 2025), using MAE in seconds. RL discovery edits the GRPO loss (Shao et al., 2024) and rollout filtering for Qwen2.5-Coder policies (Hui et al., 2024). The five RL sources train 1.5B policies on the same task with different seeds; the larger-scale instance trains a 3B policy and evaluates pass@1 on a 423-problem LiveCodeBench partition (Jain et al., 2024). Appendices A.1–A.3 specify the three protocols.

Transfer beyond discovery instances.  Track A evaluates designs beyond the discovery instances: KuaiVideo for ranking, VK-LSVD for watch-time prediction, and 632 LiveCodeBench tasks disjoint from the larger-scale selection partition for RL. The two recommendation datasets are excluded from source search, peer evaluation, and promotion. KuaiVideo also changes the objective from next-item ranking to candidate-conditioned click-through rate (CTR) prediction. Recommendation retraining uses a shared configuration calibrated and scored on each target’s released test split, without candidate-specific redesign or tuning. RL evaluation uses held-out coding tasks. These evaluations supplement the 34 core instances; Appendix F specifies selection, calibration, and reporting.

3.2 Decomposed discovery (Track B)

Track B evaluates whether discovery on small training subsets produces effective model and training designs for an expensive full target within a compute budget.

Training hierarchy. LLM and VLM pretraining each have five source instances, two intermediate instances, and one full-target instance (16 instances in total; Figure 1(c)). The hierarchy tests transfer across training subsets and training scales before committing to expensive full-target evaluation. The sources include three disjoint 5% subsets, D5-A/B/C. D2-A and D2-B each contain 2% of the target corpus and are nested in D5-A and D5-B, respectively. Disjoint peers test whether gains persist beyond the source subset; the nested 2%/5% instances test transfer across data volumes and numbers of training steps. Two approximately 10% intermediate instances test different forms of transfer: D10 clean uses data disjoint from every source, while D10+C combines D5-C with a fresh 5% subset. Requiring success on both is intended to prioritize designs whose gains persist under full-target training. Full-target evaluation uses 100% of the training corpus. The same executable intervention is evaluated at each tier under its prescribed training configuration.

Pretraining tasks. LLM discovery starts from a 185M-parameter Gemma 3-style decoder (Gemma Team, 2025) and can modify its architecture, optimizer, and training mechanisms. Training uses the FineWeb-Edu 100B core set (Lozhkov et al., 2024; Karpathy, 2025). The score is mean accuracy over the seven zero-shot tasks used in Mamba-2 (Dao & Gu, 2024): ARC-Challenge, ARC-Easy, HellaSwag, LAMBADA OpenAI, OpenBookQA, PIQA, and WinoGrande. VLM discovery edits a Qwen3.5-style backbone (Qwen Team, 2026), projector, optimizer, and schedule, retaining a frozen SigLIP encoder (Zhai et al., 2023). The starting VLM has approximately 646M trainable parameters; full-target training uses 2.38M raw FineVisionMax-format examples (Wiedmann et al., 2025). The score is token-weighted validation cross-entropy. Appendices A.4 and A.5 give the full specifications.

3.3 Evaluation and reporting

Each intervention is evaluated by training a model under the receiving instance’s prescribed initialization, data, and training allocation. For candidate score ye​(h)y_{e}(h) and fixed reference score beb_{e} on instance ee, relative improvement is

re​(h)=se​(ye​(h)−be)max⁡(|be|,ϵ),r_{e}(h)=\frac{s_{e}\bigl(y_{e}(h)-b_{e}\bigr)}{\max(|b_{e}|,\epsilon)}, (2)

where se=+1s_{e}=+1 for ranking score or accuracy and −1-1 for MAE or loss; ϵ>0\epsilon>0 prevents division by zero. Reported percentage gains are 100​re​(h)100r_{e}(h). Track A reports local gains, larger-scale transfer, and transfer beyond discovery instances. Track B reports full-target quality and discovery yield: the number of candidates meeting predefined full-training success criteria. Section 4 specifies the comparisons; Appendices A.7, A.8, and B.5 describe baseline calibration, discovery compute scales, and budget accounting.

4 Experiments

Experiments test local discovery and transfer in Track A, and full-target quality and completed-run yield in Track B. Section 5 analyzes peer evaluation and shared evidence.

4.1 Experimental setup and comparisons

Shared protocols. The main experiments use the AdaEvolve-based search harness (Cemri et al., 2026) with GPT-5.5 at high reasoning effort as the proposer (Appendix B). Methods share starting models, reference configurations, editable interfaces, instructions, and training/evaluation protocols (Appendix A.6). Gains use fixed instance references (Equation 2). Section 4.4 varies the harness and proposer in watch-time discovery.

Track A: independent and collaborative discovery. Standalone evolution (S) runs independent source searches using the same harness and parent-selection rules as PE, without shared context. Both methods run five 100-iteration searches. Table 2A–C compares locally proposed candidates with and without shared feedback; peer-replayed candidates are reported separately (Section 5.1). Local recommendation results average the best gain from each dataset; RL uses the best result across five searches of the same task. At larger scale, S retrains each source’s top candidates by source performance, while PE retrains promoted candidates. S’s per-source quota is rounded up to give it at least as many larger-scale evaluations as PE (Table 2D). Neither method searches locally at larger scale. Transfer evaluations use shared target protocols without candidate-specific redesign or tuning (Appendix F.1).

Track B: hierarchical discovery under a compute budget. PE screens candidates from five subset searches at intermediate scale before full training; direct evolution (Direct) runs five full-target searches. Completed runs use matched total GPU compute within each family. PE proposals use only source and intermediate feedback; Direct uses full-target feedback (Appendix B.5).

4.2 Joint discovery improves local quality and generalization

We examine local gains, transfer within the discovery hierarchy, and transfer to new datasets or tasks.

Shared feedback improves mean best local recommendation gains. At the matched source allocation, PE raises mean best local gains from 7.01% to 8.97% in ranking and 2.84% to 3.85% in watch-time, exceeding S on 3/5 and 4/5 datasets, respectively (Table 2). PE’s mean gains over calibrated starting models are non-trivial in magnitude, comparable to published improvements over the strongest reported baselines on public datasets: 0.71–12.15% in NDCG@10 for FuXi-Linear (Ye et al., 2026) and 1.72–5.04% in MAE for EGMN (Zhao et al., 2025). The best RL source gain rises from 23.53% to 32.35% (Table 2C).

Selected designs improve larger-scale outcomes. After larger-scale retraining without local search, PE yields more successful evaluations than S and raises best gains from 4.70% to 6.19% in ranking, 1.77% to 2.17% in watch-time, and 1.95% to 6.64% in RL (Table 2D). These larger-scale instances participate in discovery; we next evaluate transfer to new datasets and tasks.

Recommendation designs transfer to new datasets. Under shared target-side calibration, every evaluated PE recommendation design improves on the reference in mean performance (Appendices F.2 and F.3). PE also achieves better candidate-set means on both targets (Table 3A). The best individual design comes from S on VK-LSVD and PE on KuaiVideo.

For RL, the best PE and S candidates achieve 23.10% and 22.94% pass@1 on held-out LiveCodeBench-632 (LCB-632; Table 3B), both below the unmodified reference mean of 23.26% (Appendix F.4).

4.3 Decomposed discovery improves full-target quality and discovery yield

We compare search depth, full-target quality, and yield in completed runs under matched total GPU compute.

Subset training sustains deeper search. Under these budgets, PE completes 100 iterations per source search, compared with 14 LLM or 20 VLM iterations per full-target search for Direct. Source and intermediate feedback guide candidate refinement before full-target training.

LLM: full-target quality and completed-run yield. PE’s best full-target relative accuracy gain is 2.48%, versus 0.92% for Direct (Figure 6a). At the predefined 1% threshold, PE yields 13 successful candidates from 39 full-target attempts; Direct yields none from 70 (Table 4). PE returns more successful candidates at all four examined thresholds from 0.5% to 2% (Appendix E.3).

VLM: gains in both model quality and discovery yield. PE improves best full-target loss reduction from 5.05% to 8.78%. PE yields 57 successful candidates from 61 full-target attempts, versus 12 from 100 for Direct (Table 4). These results support affordable subset search with screening before full-target training (final-stage outcomes across families: Appendix E.1).

Successful LLM designs span several intervention types.  The 13 successful LLM candidates span changes to Muon update geometry, RoPE configurations within the existing hybrid attention stack, and late-training checkpoint averaging. Section 5.2 follows one discovery; Appendix D groups the mechanisms and lists designs from all five families (Table 23).

4.4 Applicability across search harnesses and proposal models

For watch-time discovery from EGMN, we vary the harness or proposer while holding the other fixed in matched PE/S comparisons (Appendix E.2, Table 25). PE improves the best larger-scale gain with 4/5 harnesses and, with AdaEvolve fixed, all four proposers. With Claude Opus 5, the gain rises from 2.61% to 3.64%. PE improves mean best local gains with 4/5 harnesses and 2/4 proposers. With both Opus proposers, PE has lower local means but better larger-scale outcomes than S; it improves best local gains on at least three of five datasets with every proposer.

5 Analysis: How Collaboration Supports Discovery

We compare local S–PE proposals with and without shared feedback (Section 4.2), measure direct reuse through peer replay (Section 5.1), and examine reconstructed traces of evidence availability and subsequent refinement (Section 5.2).

5.1 Peer discoveries support direct reuse and inform promotion

Direct reuse improves results beyond locally proposed candidates. We compare PE’s best locally proposed candidate (Table 2A–B) with its best available candidate after replaying peer discoveries on the same instance. Including replayed peer candidates improves PE’s best available gains on three of five ranking and one of five watch-time datasets, raising PE’s mean best gains from 8.97% to 11.29% and 3.85% to 3.95%, respectively (Appendix C, Table 21). A KuaiRand-Pure ranking candidate raises KuaiSAR’s best available PE gain from 3.88% to 10.06%; a WeChat watch-time candidate raises KuaiRand-Pure’s from 0.16% to 0.65%. Replay results inform proposals, while each search continues to select parents from its local archive (Section 2.2). Benefits vary by dataset; with peer candidates, the mean PE–S difference stays positive when any dataset is omitted (Appendix C).

Cross-instance and larger-scale evidence guide which designs advance. Figure 2 compares three individual PE designs, each retrained unchanged on its source, four peers, and larger-scale KuaiRand-27K. The KuaiRand-Pure ranking candidate improves all four peers and gains 3.02% at larger scale (a). The KuaiLive ranking candidate improves KuaiRand-1K by 10.66% but declines by 0.79% at larger scale (b). The WeChat watch-time head reduces larger-scale MAE by 2.17% despite regressing on CIKM16 (c). All three pass peer screening, but only two retain positive gains at larger scale. Peer evaluation identifies reusable designs; larger-scale evaluation checks whether their gains persist.

5.2 Tracing shared evidence and subsequent local refinement

The LLM case reconstructs available shared evidence and traces subsequent local adaptations of established techniques; a complementary watch-time reuse case appears in Appendix D.1.

Shared checkpoint averaging and continued local development.

In LLM pretraining, a D2-B candidate implements checkpoint averaging using exponential moving average (EMA) and stochastic weight averaging (SWA) (Izmailov et al., 2018). Replay yields a 1.43% relative accuracy gain on D5-B. Reconstructing context from archived records and the selection rule indicates availability before proposal 59. Proposal 59 uses checkpoint averaging late in training. Proposal 89 later restricts averaging to approximately the final 20% of training. Proposals 59 and 89 gain 0.90% and 2.48%, respectively, over the fixed full-target reference. Proposal 89 raises accuracy from its direct parent’s 41.13% to 41.25% (Table 24). Full-target outcomes were withheld from proposal feedback.

6 Related Work

Architecture search, Population-Based Training, and AutoML-Zero automate model and algorithm design (Real et al., 2019; Jaderberg et al., 2017; Real et al., 2020). LLM-guided search enables flexible code edits (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024; Novikov et al., 2025; Lange et al., 2025), while quality-diversity methods maintain diverse candidates (Mouret & Clune, 2015; Nasir et al., 2024). Evolutionary multitasking and multi-task architecture search transfer knowledge across tasks (Gupta et al., 2016; Liao et al., 2024; Zhang & Liu, 2025); AgentRxiv shares research reports (Schmidgall & Moor, 2025). FunSearch uses islands to maintain diverse populations for one target problem (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024). EMO-STA evolves a shared archive before adapting selected programs to individual tasks (Gozeten et al., 2026). PE maintains ongoing task-specific searches and archives, sharing executable interventions and peer evaluation results to guide local edits and cross-scale promotion.

NASNet transfers architectures from CIFAR-10 to ImageNet (Zoph et al., 2018), while FABOLAS varies dataset size during hyperparameter optimization (Klein et al., 2017). AlphaEvolve uses evaluation cascades (Novikov et al., 2025); multi-fidelity methods allocate evaluation resources (Li et al., 2018; Trofimov et al., 2020), and Janus co-evolves proxy evaluators (Liu et al., 2026c). PE combines affordable local search, peer and intermediate screening, and full-target verification.

Existing benchmarks cover competitions and ML experimentation (Chan et al., 2024; Nathani et al., 2025), multi-GPU/multi-node experiments (Wu et al., 2025), and paper-derived research tasks in ResearchGym (Garikaparthi et al., 2026). Others cover post-training (Rank et al., 2026), adaptive pretraining budgets (Lyu et al., 2026), or open-ended tasks (Zhu et al., 2026). RMD-Bench evaluates collaboration across ongoing local searches and discovery across training scales, including transfer to new datasets and tasks in Track A and full-target quality and yield in Track B (Table 1).

7 Conclusion

Population Evolution connects searches through shared evidence and hierarchical promotion; RMD-Bench supplies executable evaluation protocols. Shared feedback improves mean best local recommendation gains; peer replay enables reuse. PE improves best larger-scale outcomes, and its recommendation designs transfer to new datasets. Under matched total GPU compute, hierarchical discovery improves full-target LLM/VLM quality and completed-run yield. Watch-time best larger-scale gains improve with four of five harnesses and all four proposers. Appendix G discusses limitations and future directions.

AI use statement

The authors wrote most of the manuscript and supplied its key scientific points, numerical results, and technical details. Generative AI tools were used in a supporting role to draft and polish selected passages, retrieve related literature, and provide feedback on methodology and result interpretation. LLM-driven proposal and code generation within the discovery experiments are described in Section 2 and Appendix B. The authors reviewed and revised AI-assisted content and made the final scientific and editorial decisions, taking full responsibility for the final text, claims, results, and research artifacts.

Reproducibility statement

Appendix A specifies the datasets, preprocessing, starting models, editable components, training and evaluation protocols, and baseline calibration used in RMD-Bench. Appendix B documents PE’s publication and promotion criteria, shared proposal context, prompts, asynchronous search procedure, and evaluation accounting. Appendix F details candidate selection, target calibration, reference scores, and repeated transfer evaluations. Appendices C and E report per-instance outcomes and additional configuration and budget comparisons. The benchmark and search code will be made publicly available.
