Appendix A RMD-Bench Specifications and Evaluation Protocols

This appendix specifies the data, starting model, editable interface, and evaluation protocol for each task family in Section 3. Table 5 summarizes the five families; the following subsections give their protocols, baseline calibration, and discovery compute scales. Counts describe the processed inputs used in our experiments and can differ from the original public releases. Following Section 2, source instances host local search, intermediate instances provide Track B screening and feedback, and larger-scale or full-target instances assess selected designs. Each PE source search receives 100 iterations. Appendix F specifies the additional evaluations of selected designs beyond these discovery instances. For error and loss objectives, a harness that maximizes fitness receives the negative metric; reported values and promotion retain the original lower-is-better metric.

A.1 Sequential ranking

Data and preprocessing.

The source family comprises KuaiLive (Qu et al., 2025), KuaiRand-1K and KuaiRand-Pure (Gao et al., 2022b), KuaiRec (Gao et al., 2022a), and KuaiSAR (Sun et al., 2023). KuaiLive treats clicked streamers as items. KuaiSAR uses clicked interactions from recommendation pages. For each user or session, interactions are ordered chronologically; the last interaction is the next-item target, and preceding interactions form the history. KuaiRand ranking uses the processed standard-exposure logs. The benchmark evaluates full-catalog next-item ranking.

Starting model and training.

The reference is FuXi-Linear (Ye et al., 2026), with positional and temporal channels and a causal chunkwise implementation (Table 7). User and item embeddings are L2-normalized and scored by dot product. Training uses autoregressive sampled softmax and AdamW. Baseline HPO selects dropout, learning rate, per-GPU batch size, and weight decay separately for each dataset (Appendix A.7). Table 6 gives the resulting training allocations, and Table 16 lists the selected hyperparameters.

Editable interface.

The proposer can jointly modify three components:

  • •

    FuXi-Linear blocks, channels, and the user representation.

  • •

    Retention, temporal interactions, normalization, and gating.

  • •

    The causal chunkwise attention kernel.

The input/output interfaces and the training path from user representations to sampled-softmax loss remain intact. Data loading, loss, sampling, and evaluation are fixed. KuaiRand-1K additionally uses the per-candidate HPO procedure in Appendix A.7; the other four sources use fixed optimizer settings.

Evaluation and promotion.

The ranking score used as evolutionary fitness is

Rrank=(NDCG​@​10+HR​@​10+MRR)/3.R_{\mathrm{rank}}=(\mathrm{NDCG@10}+\mathrm{HR@10}+\mathrm{MRR})/3.

Published interventions are retrained on the four peer datasets, and candidates meeting the peer criterion advance to KuaiRand-27K for larger-scale evaluation. Table 20 specifies publication, peer, and larger-scale success thresholds; standalone top-kk candidates use the same larger-scale evaluator and success criterion.

A.2 Watch-time prediction

Data and preprocessing.

The source datasets are CIKM16 (CIKM Cup, ), KuaiRec (Gao et al., 2022a), WeChat, KuaiRand-Pure, and KuaiRand-1K (Gao et al., 2022b), with KuaiRand-27K as the larger-scale evaluation instance. Following EGMN (Zhao et al., 2025), we include CIKM16 as a related engagement-duration task: its labels describe time spent in online search sessions. Training uses a fixed deterministic 80% partition; the remaining 20% supplies the evaluation scores used throughout discovery. Within each dataset, all methods share a p99 label scale estimated from the processed corpus before partitioning. KuaiRand watch-time preprocessing combines random- and standard-exposure logs. KuaiRec and KuaiRand-27K use sampled processed corpora. Table 8 reports processed examples rather than original-release interactions.

Starting model and training.

EGMN (Zhao et al., 2025) uses 16-dimensional sparse and sequence embeddings, mean-pooled sequence features, linear projections of continuous features, and a 256–128–64 MLP encoder. Its starting head combines one exponential component for fast skips and ten non-negative left-truncated Gaussian components. The point prediction is the mixture expectation. The starting model’s objective combines the mixture negative log-likelihood with entropy and absolute-error terms weighted by α\alpha and β\beta:

ℒ=ℒmixture​NLL+α​ℒentropy+β​|y^−y|.\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mixture\ NLL}}+\alpha\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{entropy}}+\beta|\hat{y}-y|.

Runs use Adagrad, 10 epochs, batch size 2,048, and a fixed training seed. The S and PE runs with GPT-5.5 share the HPO-selected configurations in Table 9, with per-candidate HPO disabled; Appendix A.7 specifies calibration.

Editable interface and fitness.

Only the watch-time prediction head is evolvable. Its search space includes likelihood parameterization, mixture components, point prediction, and duration conditioning. All candidates share the feature encoder, data pipeline, optimizer settings, epoch count, batch size, and evaluator. The evaluation metric is MAE (lower is better), reported in seconds on this partition using the fixed p99 label scale in Table 8. Candidates advance through peer and larger-scale evaluation using the MAE-reduction criteria in Table 20.

A.3 RL algorithm discovery

Source and larger-scale instances.

The five source instances differ only in the training random seed. Each uses Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B-Instruct (Hui et al., 2024), 15 GRPO steps, and the same 408-problem DeepCoder Codeforces/test partition (Luo et al., 2025). The larger-scale instance uses Qwen2.5-Coder-3B-Instruct, 50 steps, and a disjoint 423-problem LiveCodeBench partition (Jain et al., 2024). This partition is a deterministic platform-by-difficulty stratified selection from a 1,055-problem snapshot. Table 10 summarizes the source and larger-scale training and evaluation settings.

The RL training pool has 16,252 DeepCoder primeintellect/train examples and 7,436 taco/train examples, totaling 23,688 problems. After normalizing prompt text, we find no exact overlap between the training and evaluation prompts and retain all training examples. Every candidate starts from the same pretrained policy weights, without inheriting trained weights from earlier search iterations.

Training and search space.

The RL protocol disables HPO and fixes Adam with learning rate 10−610^{-6}, a low-variance KL estimator with coefficient 0.001, and clipping coefficients 0.2/0.28.

Editable interface.

Evolution can modify the GRPO loss through changes to surrogate-loss geometry, clipping treatment, KL treatment, and advantage weighting, and can modify rollout filtering through the selection, weighting, or rejection of rollout groups. It cannot change the model, training corpus, learning rate, fixed clipping/KL coefficients, RL horizon, rollout batch, response count, or evaluator.

Two reward levels.

Within candidate training, a sampled program receives the fraction of unit tests passed, with a −0.1-0.1 penalty for unparseable or truncated output. The outer evolutionary fitness is code-generation pass@1 under deterministic decoding: the number of solved evaluation problems divided by the partition size. Evaluation generates one completion per problem, with the evaluator’s test cases excluded from the generation prompt. The larger-scale evaluator uses hidden private tests. The fixed reference score is the arithmetic mean of three valid baseline repetitions.

Promotion and reported outcomes.

Table 20 gives the joint relative and absolute improvement criteria for publication, peer validation, and larger-scale success. The larger-scale evaluation measures transfer jointly across policy size, training horizon, and code benchmark. The five RL sources share the same task, training data, and objective and differ only in random seed. We therefore treat them as parallel searches for the strongest algorithm and report the best outcome across the five searches.

A.4 LLM pretraining

Data hierarchy.

The benchmark uses the FineWeb-Edu 100B core set from the shuffled release (Lozhkov et al., 2024; Karpathy, 2025). Table 11 gives the exact corpus inventories and training allocations. Source and intermediate subsets use fixed contiguous shard ranges from the shuffled corpus. The three 5% sources D5-A/B/C are mutually disjoint; D2-A/B are 2% subsets nested within D5-A/B, respectively. D10 clean is disjoint from every source slice. D10+C combines D5-C with a fresh disjoint 5% slice, testing an increase in data around a known source. The full-target instance trains on the complete reference corpus.

Model and training.

The starting model is an approximately 185M-parameter decoder with a Gemma 3-style architecture (Gemma Team, 2025): RMSNorm, SwiGLU, RoPE, and hybrid local/global attention. The model uses the Llama 3.1 tokenizer and a context length of 1,024. Training uses eight H200 GPUs, a micro-batch size of 352, and no gradient accumulation, giving approximately 2.88M tokens per step. Each candidate is pretrained from scratch. The training-step count scales with data volume to approximate one pass through each subset; baseline hyperparameters are specified per instance in Table 17.

Editable interface.

The proposer can modify four components:

  • •

    Model architecture, including attention, normalization, and feed-forward computation.

  • •

    Muon optimizer geometry (Jordan et al., 2024), including Newton–Schulz updates, clipping, and parameter grouping.

  • •

    The Warmup–Stable–Decay learning-rate schedule.

  • •

    Training mechanisms within the fixed data and compute budget.

Dataset assignment, tokenizer, sequence length, batch size, total steps, checkpoint isolation, and evaluation are protected.

Evaluator.

We use lm-evaluation-harness (Gao et al., 2023) in zero-shot mode. ARC-Challenge and ARC-Easy (Clark et al., 2018), HellaSwag (Zellers et al., 2019), and OpenBookQA (Mihaylov et al., 2018) use normalized accuracy. PIQA (Bisk et al., 2019), WinoGrande (Sakaguchi et al., 2019), and the OpenAI variant of LAMBADA (Paperno et al., 2016) use standard accuracy. The evaluator loads the final checkpoint and takes the unweighted mean of these seven scores. All seven evaluations must return successfully, and the implementation must pass the causal-leakage check, for a run to be valid. Decomposed PE excludes full-target outcomes from adaptive proposal feedback; direct full-target evolution uses those outcomes during search.

Publication and promotion.

Published candidates must pass peer screening and both intermediate evaluations before full-target training. Table 20 specifies the improvement thresholds at each stage and the full-target graduation criterion.

A.5 VLM pretraining

Data hierarchy.

The benchmark uses a 1,000-shard image–conversation corpus in FineVisionMax format (Wiedmann et al., 2025). Shards 980–999 define the validation split; the full target uses the remaining 980 training shards. Table 12 gives the source, intermediate, and full-target inventories.

Model and training.

The language backbone is a custom 28-layer hybrid decoder with a Qwen3.5-style architecture (Qwen Team, 2026), including full grouped-query attention and causal-convolutional linear attention, RMSNorm, SwiGLU, and RoPE. A frozen SigLIP-so400m-patch14-384 encoder (Zhai et al., 2023) supplies 729 image-token positions per image; a trainable two-layer MLP projects these features into the language model. The model has approximately 641.6M parameters in the language backbone, 646.1M trainable parameters including the projector, and 1.074B total parameters including the frozen vision encoder.

Training uses eight H200 GPUs, a micro-batch size of 8, gradient accumulation over 16 steps, a sequence length of 2,048, and BF16 precision. Step counts scale with subset size to approximate one training epoch, ranging from 48 to 2,320. Each candidate trains the language backbone and projector from scratch with the frozen vision encoder; evolved candidates do not inherit learned weights from earlier iterations.

Editable interface.

The proposer can modify three components:

  • •

    The language backbone’s attention, normalization, RoPE, and SwiGLU blocks, and the MLP projector.

  • •

    Optimizer updates, orthogonalization, Q/K clipping, and parameter grouping.

  • •

    The Warmup–Stable–Decay learning-rate schedule.

The frozen SigLIP encoder, projector width, image-token interface, outer fusion/data path, data assignment, sequence length, batch and accumulation, steps, and evaluator remain fixed.

Evaluation metric and validity.

The evaluator measures token-weighted next-token cross-entropy on validation data disjoint from training. Before scoring, the evaluator verifies the frozen vision encoder, parameter budget, and causal validity. The shifted next-token objective predicts position t+1t+1 from position tt; masked positions are excluded from the supervised loss. The reported loss sums cross-entropy over these supervised tokens and divides by their total count, rather than averaging example losses.

Graduation.

Candidates advance after peer screening and must pass both intermediate evaluations before full-target training. Table 20 specifies the relative and absolute loss-reduction criteria at each stage. Decomposed PE withholds full-target outcomes from adaptive search feedback.

A.6 Shared task guidance

Preliminary experiments identify recurring implementation errors, which we summarize in shared domain guidance. All compared discovery methods receive the same guidance for a given task family in every LLM call. Table 13 summarizes the guidance; Appendix B.3 shows how it accompanies task instructions and shared evidence.

A.7 Baseline calibration and per-candidate hyperparameter optimization

Baseline calibration before discovery.

Baseline HPO tunes the unmodified starting implementation separately for each instance before evolutionary search. Ranking, watch-time, and LLM/VLM source and intermediate references use CMA-ES sampling in Optuna (Akiba et al., 2019), with LLM-proposed configurations added after warm-up when the trial budget permits. Results from all evaluated configurations update the CMA-ES search. Tables 14 and 15 specify the calibration settings, trial caps, and search spaces. The starting code, model capacity, data, evaluator, and prescribed epochs or step count remain fixed during calibration; ranking additionally searches the per-GPU batch size. The selected configuration and measured reference score are then fixed and shared by competing discovery procedures in that instance. RL disables baseline HPO and uses the mean of three independent fixed-configuration runs in each source and larger-scale instance. LLM and VLM full targets each use one measured reference under a prescribed configuration shared by PE and Direct. The cost of full-target training precludes a separate full-target HPO sweep within the study budget; both methods use the same full-target reference and evaluation protocol.

Selected configurations.

Table 16 gives the selected ranking hyperparameters, and Table 9 lists the six watch-time configurations. Table 17 gives the LLM/VLM source, intermediate, and full-target configurations. The fixed RL configuration is specified in Appendix A.3.

Per-candidate HPO in the reported configuration.

Per-candidate HPO adapts training hyperparameters for a proposed intervention during discovery and is separate from baseline calibration. Per-candidate HPO is enabled only for KuaiRand-1K ranking, using the same procedure for PE and standalone evolution. We enable it on this instance because performance is particularly sensitive to training hyperparameters and the small dataset makes repeated tuning affordable. Table 18 records the reported GPT-5.5 settings, including the extra trials and optional paired baseline control.

Paired baseline control and selection.

After a successful main evaluation, per-candidate HPO starts from the receiving instance’s calibrated baseline hyperparameters. When a paired control is used, it evaluates the unmodified code under the candidate’s selected hyperparameters, yielding b~e​(h)\widetilde{b}_{e}(h) for candidate hh on instance ee. This control measures the code intervention’s effect at the candidate’s selected hyperparameters. Source publication retains the ordinary source rule in Table 20 and, when a valid paired control exists, additionally requires the candidate to exceed that control by the prescribed relative improvement margin. Cross-instance selection uses the stronger of the fixed reference and any valid paired control:

se​begate​(h)=max⁡{se​be,se​b~e​(h)}.s_{e}b_{e}^{\mathrm{gate}}(h)=\max\{s_{e}b_{e},\,s_{e}\widetilde{b}_{e}(h)\}. (3)

When no valid paired control is available, we set begate​(h)=beb_{e}^{\mathrm{gate}}(h)=b_{e}. Thus begate​(h)b_{e}^{\mathrm{gate}}(h) is the larger reference for reward/accuracy and the smaller reference for error/loss. Reported gains still use the fixed reference beb_{e} (Equation 2); cross-instance selection uses begate​(h)b_{e}^{\mathrm{gate}}(h).

A.8 Discovery compute and search depth

We report compute for a complete discovery run, comprising five parallel searches and their prescribed evaluations. Due to policy restrictions, we cannot disclose exact GPU-hour usage; Table 19 reports the permitted orders of magnitude. LLM and VLM pretraining require thousands of GPU-hours per complete run, ranking and RL algorithm discovery require hundreds, and watch-time prediction requires tens. The benchmark and search code will be made publicly available to support reproduction under the stated protocols.

PE uses smaller training subsets for ongoing proposal–evaluation cycles and reserves full-target training for candidates that pass the peer and intermediate gates. Appendix B.5 specifies the completed-run comparison and accounts for all executed search and evaluation stages.

Appendix B Population Evolution Implementation and Reporting

This appendix connects the search procedure in Section 2 to its implementation. We specify publication and promotion decisions, the evidence supplied to each source search, and asynchronous execution, then define the units used to report compute and outcomes.

B.1 Publication and promotion thresholds

PE tests publication and promotion margins against the reference score of the instance being evaluated. Based on preliminary studies, we set domain-specific margins to require challenging but attainable improvements under the prescribed training allocations and fix them for the reported comparisons. These margins define operational promotion and success criteria; Tables 2 and 4 also report continuous performance gains. Source publication requires the configured gain over the fixed reference and, when a valid paired control is available, the additional gain over that control (Appendix A.7). Cross-instance selection uses the gating reference begate​(h)b_{e}^{\mathrm{gate}}(h) defined in Equation 3. With ses_{e} defined in Equation 2, the directed absolute gain is aegate​(h)=se​(ye​(h)−begate​(h))a_{e}^{\mathrm{gate}}(h)=s_{e}\bigl(y_{e}(h)-b_{e}^{\mathrm{gate}}(h)\bigr) and the relative gain is regate​(h)=aegate​(h)/max⁡(|begate​(h)|,ϵ)r_{e}^{\mathrm{gate}}(h)=a_{e}^{\mathrm{gate}}(h)/\max(|b_{e}^{\mathrm{gate}}(h)|,\epsilon). An evaluation passes only when the run is valid, the score is finite, and every configured relative and absolute margin is met. For an intervention hh originating at EiE_{i}, let ρx\rho_{x} and αx\alpha_{x} denote the configured relative and absolute peer margins, and let KxK_{x} be the required number of passing peers. Counting only completed valid peer evaluations, the selector implements

eligible(h)=[∑Ej∈𝒟∖{Ei}[rjgate(h)≥ρx∧ajgate(h)≥αx]≥Kx].\operatorname{eligible}(h)=\mathbf{1}\!\left[\sum_{E_{j}\in\mathcal{D}\setminus\{E_{i}\}}\mathbf{1}\!\left[r_{j}^{\mathrm{gate}}(h)\geq\rho_{x}\ \land\ a_{j}^{\mathrm{gate}}(h)\geq\alpha_{x}\right]\geq K_{x}\right]. (4)

An omitted margin imposes no constraint; in our experiments, Kx=2K_{x}=2 for every domain. Scores are not averaged across instances before selection. An eligible candidate proceeds to the larger-scale instance in Track A or to the two intermediate instances in Track B. Both intermediate instances must pass before full-target training. Graduation then requires the Track A larger-scale or Track B full-target margin. Table 20 specifies the margins used by PE; the benchmark’s training and evaluation instances can also support other selection policies.

B.2 Shared candidate records and search context

The shared ledger connects candidate evaluation to ongoing local search. A source publishes a promising intervention, peers evaluate it, and the accumulated results enter later proposal prompts (Figure 1(a)). The following describes this information flow; Appendix B.3 shows how it enters proposal prompts and candidate construction.

Publishing a candidate.

After a candidate meets its source instance’s publication margin (Appendix B.1), PE creates a shared record containing the executable intervention and a short description of its mechanism. The record identifies the source instance and iteration, reports its score and reference baseline, and tracks the candidate’s evaluation results and current status. The record keeps executable code distinct from the mechanism description: peer evaluation executes the code, while proposal context summarizes the mechanism and its measured outcomes.

Evaluating the intervention on peers.

For each peer, the coordinator restores that instance’s reference implementation, applies the published intervention, and runs the peer’s prescribed training and evaluation. Model parameters are trained separately under the receiving instance’s protocol. This cross-instance replay measures where the published intervention remains useful. Each completed evaluation adds the receiving instance, score, gain, and pass decision to the candidate’s record. Valid weak or near-neutral results remain available even when they do not meet a promotion margin. The completed peer results determine eligibility for larger-scale or intermediate evaluation under the criteria in Appendix B.1.

Building context for the next local proposal.

Before each LLM call on source instance EiE_{i}, PE selects relevant records from the ledger to form the shared context Φi​(Mt)\Phi_{i}(M_{t}) in Equation 1. This context contains three groups:

  • •

    Own candidates: at most ten candidates published by EiE_{i}, with available peer and larger-scale or intermediate results.

  • •

    Successful peer transfers: at most six candidates from other source instances that succeeded on EiE_{i}, ranked by their measured benefit on EiE_{i}.

  • •

    Weak or unsuccessful peer transfers: at most six candidates from other source instances that failed or transferred weakly on EiE_{i}.

Each selected entry summarizes the mechanism, originating instance, evaluation status, and measured effects; all entries together are limited to 4K tokens. Gains are direction-normalized as in Equation 2, so positive values indicate improvement for both accuracy and loss metrics. The local harness retains its own program archive, while the proposer uses the shared evidence to reuse, modify, or combine mechanisms in later candidates. This separates two uses of shared records: replay tests an existing intervention, while proposal context helps generate the next one.

B.3 Prompts and local code edits

Each source instance uses a local search harness to select a parent program and ask an LLM for a code edit. The main experiments use the AdaEvolve-based implementation in SkyDiscover (Liu et al., 2026b; Cemri et al., 2026). At each proposal step, the prompt combines the local program and search history with the shared context described in Appendix B.2.

Inputs to the proposer.

The template combines fixed task instructions and shared domain guidance with the selected parent, local history, and latest available shared evidence.

SYSTEM
  Objective, dataset, metric, and fixed training budget
  Editable regions, interfaces, and fixed controls
  Shared context: own candidates and their transfer results
                  peer candidates evaluated on this instance
  Domain guidance and harness tool instructions

USER
  Selected parent code and metrics
  Previous attempts and evaluator feedback
  Program examples sampled by the harness
  Search objective and edit requirements

Example of the shared context.

Consider a proposal on VLM source instance D2-A. Its shared context can include the candidate discovered on D5-C at iteration 55 and subsequently evaluated on D2-A. The intervention replaces global Muon gradient clipping with clipping based on the final update’s RMS, yielding relative gains of approximately 10.50% on D5-C and 10.34% on D2-A.

Candidate from a peer instance
  Source: VLM D5-C, iteration 55
  Mechanism: final-update RMS trust clipping for Muon
  Source gain: +10.50%; gain on VLM D2-A: +10.34%
  Receiving-instance decision: pass
  Full-target outcomes: withheld from proposal context

In this Track B example, the proposer receives peer and intermediate evidence but no full-target scores or pass/fail outcomes (Figure 1(c)). The task objectives, editable components, and fixed experimental controls follow Appendices A.1–A.5.

Output: a local edit to the selected parent.

The LLM edits the selected parent within the permitted components, preserving the specified interfaces and fixed experimental controls. The candidate is then trained and evaluated on its source instance. The evaluation updates the local history and archive; candidates meeting the publication margin enter the shared ledger for cross-instance replay (Appendix B.2).

B.4 Asynchronous discovery loop

Algorithm 1 summarizes the population operations. Local searches and evaluation jobs proceed asynchronously. Each source harness refreshes its shared-evidence context before every LLM call. Iteration numbers are local to each source; timestamps determine which shared results are available to a proposal.

B.5 Execution accounting and evidence units

Iterations, evaluations, and complete runs.

A source iteration is one local proposal–evaluation cycle. A complete discovery run comprises five source searches for PE or five independent searches for S/Direct, together with their prescribed transfer and target evaluations. Discovery compute includes local search, peer replay, intermediate screening, and final-stage evaluation. Per-candidate HPO trials, paired controls, retries, failed attempts, and re-evaluations are charged to discovery compute. Shared baseline calibration is performed before search and accounted for separately.

Comparison budgets.

Track A matches source iterations; Track B compares completed PE and Direct runs under matched total GPU compute across all stages. For Track A larger-scale evaluation, S selects the top k=⌈NPE/5⌉k=\lceil N_{\mathrm{PE}}/5\rceil candidates by source score from each of its five searches, where NPEN_{\mathrm{PE}} is the number of PE larger-scale candidate evaluations. Rounding up gives S at least as many larger-scale candidate evaluations as PE. Allocated compute sums GPU count multiplied by training–evaluation runtime across all jobs. Exact GPU-hour usage is restricted by policy; Appendix A.8 reports the compute scales and code-release commitment. Table 4 and both panels of Figure 6 summarize the completed runs; the LLM runs have 39 full-target attempts for PE and 70 candidate-mutation attempts for Direct.

Outcome summaries.

For Track A, ranking and watch-time average each source’s best local gain across distinct datasets, whereas RL reports the best gain across five parallel searches of the same task (Table 21). Peer-evaluation results and larger-scale outcomes are summarized separately. Track B reports the best full-target gain and the number of successful candidates from each completed run, using the criteria in Table 20. Comparisons and relative gains are computed before display rounding. Reported gains always use the fixed reference in Equation 2; paired controls can strengthen selection without redefining this reference. Appendix B.6 gives raw attempt counts and passing means.

Replication.

Given the substantial training cost of complete discovery runs, we report one complete run per method–configuration and allocate the available compute to comparisons across task families and model proposers. The five searches are components of one complete run; repeated baseline evaluations estimate the reference score rather than variation across discovery runs. For the configurations examined in preliminary independent runs, the relative performance ordering was consistent across runs.

B.6 Full-target outcome details

Each candidate contributes at most one success, regardless of repeated evaluations.

LLM outcomes.

Over its completed run, PE evaluates 39 candidates in 39 full-target attempts; 34 return numeric scores and five return no score. Thirteen meet the success criterion, with a mean gain of 1.67% among the successful candidates. Attempts without a score remain in the attempt count and do not contribute a success. Direct produces no successful candidates from 70 candidate-mutation attempts; this count excludes the five initialization evaluations. Both methods’ outcomes are reported after their complete discovery runs under matched total GPU compute (Appendix B.5). Appendix E.3 varies the full-target success threshold using these same results.

VLM outcomes.

Direct completes 100 attempts across five searches, with 96 finite scores and four failed attempts. Seventeen evaluations meet the full-target criterion, corresponding to 12 successful candidates. Relative to the fixed baseline loss 1.2071, the best loss is 1.1461 (5.05% reduction) and the passing-evaluation mean is 1.1535 (4.44% reduction). PE has 61 full-target attempts, 57 finite scores, and four failed attempts. All 57 finite outcomes meet the criterion, yielding 57 successful candidates with a mean gain of 7.66%.

Appendix C Per-instance Discovery Outcomes

Table 21 reports local discovery outcomes for S and PE alongside PE’s best gains from local and replayed peer candidates (Section 5.1). For ranking and watch-time, the reported means average the best local gain on each dataset. The five RL searches share the same base model and training data and differ only in random seed. Their goal is to find the strongest algorithm for this task, so we report the best result across the five searches.

Variation across datasets.

Table 22 reports the PE–S difference on each recommendation source, separately for locally proposed candidates and for PE’s best available candidates including peer replay. PE’s local gains exceed S on three of five ranking datasets and four of five watch-time datasets, with the largest differences on KuaiLive and CIKM16. Omitting KuaiLive changes the ranking local-mean difference to approximately −1.11-1.11 percentage points; omitting CIKM16 changes the watch-time difference to approximately −0.04-0.04 points. When PE’s replayed peer candidates are included, the corresponding differences remain positive at approximately +1.79+1.79 and +0.08+0.08 points, and the mean difference remains positive after omitting any one dataset in either family. Thus local-search benefits are uneven, while direct reuse broadens the available improvements. These are descriptive aggregation checks derived from the displayed source results.

Appendix D Graduated Designs and Transfer Analysis

Table 23 illustrates one graduated design from each task family. Tables 2 and 4 report the strongest outcome in each family. The 13 successful LLM candidates span three intervention families: Muon update geometry, RoPE configurations within the existing hybrid attention stack, and late-training EMA/SWA checkpoint averaging.

Interpreting the transfer profiles.

Figure 2 shows three individual PE candidates: (a) the ranking design discovered on KuaiRand-Pure at iteration 57, (b) a ranking design discovered on KuaiLive, and (c) the watch-time head discovered on WeChat at iteration 21. The profiles measure transfer after retraining the same design under each receiving instance’s protocol; unevaluated pairs remain unknown. Figure 3 traces the availability of shared evidence and subsequent local proposals. Figure 4 evaluates the checkpoint-averaging design from D5-B iteration 89.

D.1 Execution traces and mechanism analysis

The cases use the runs underlying Tables 2 and 4, with archived candidate code, evaluation results, and proposal records supporting the mechanism analysis. The shared-context reconstruction combines archived ledger records available before each proposal with the context-selection rule; saved base prompts do not include the added shared-context text. The evaluations measure transfer, while the traces establish when evidence was available for reuse. Proposal indices are local to each source search; the sequence below follows event timing across asynchronous searches. Gains use the fixed instance reference unless a direct-parent comparison is stated.

Case 1: LLM checkpoint averaging and continued local refinement.

The D2-B iteration-100 candidate implements checkpoint averaging using EMA/SWA late in training, alongside inherited short-context RoPE and Muon update-order changes. It improves three of four peers and gains 1.06% on the full target, above the graduation threshold, while regressing by 1.12% on D2-A. The reconstructed context for D5-B proposal 59 includes this successful peer-evaluation record, which was available before the proposal. D5-B’s iteration-59 proposal adopts checkpoint averaging using EMA/SWA in a new local candidate, beginning averaging roughly 55–65% into training or during the WSD decay phase. The resulting design improves D5-B by 3.30% but gains only 0.90% on the full target, below the 1% graduation threshold. The later D5-B iteration-89 candidate averages checkpoints over approximately the final 20% of training. On the full target, this candidate reaches 41.25% accuracy, compared with 41.13% for its direct parent—a 0.28% relative improvement computed from unrounded scores (Table 24). This improvement accompanies a 1.17% source regression. Its 2.48% full-target gain is relative to the fixed 40.25% reference; iteration 59 is an earlier design in the search, not its direct parent. Full-target outcomes are excluded from proposal feedback and are used here to compare the resulting designs. Checkpoint averaging plausibly reduces sensitivity to the final optimizer iterate. The trace documents the peer evidence available before the local edits and the transfer performance of the resulting designs.

Case 2: Watch-time design reuse across datasets.

The WeChat iteration-21 watch-time head combines a duration-conditioned, left-truncated Laplace mixture with a learned near-median quantile readout. The design conditions on log⁡(1+duration)\log(1+\mathrm{duration}) and softly anchors component locations to video duration. The mixture models concentrated viewing modes and long watch times from repeated viewing, while the near-median readout aligns point prediction with absolute error. A differentiable quantile is learned within approximately [0.45,0.55][0.45,0.55], with a small mixture-dependent gate for an additional soft duration adjustment. Bisection locates the quantile, and a Newton correction propagates gradients through the distribution parameters. Relative to its parent, the combined edit reduces source MAE from 17.79 to 17.72 seconds, a 0.39% local improvement. When retrained unchanged, the complete design improves KuaiRand-Pure by 0.65%, exceeding the 0.16% gain of its best locally proposed PE candidate. It achieves the best reported larger-scale result, a 2.17% MAE reduction on KuaiRand-27K, while regressing by 2.70% on CIKM16 (Figure 2c). On VK-LSVD under shared target-side calibration, the same head reduces MAE by 1.02% across three training seeds (Appendix F.2). This case shows how PE turns a local discovery into a design useful to other instances, with benefits that extend to a dataset outside discovery.

Ranking: a local transition channel improves receiving source instances.

The KuaiRand-Pure iteration-57 candidate adds a length-64 strictly causal local attention branch alongside linear retention, combining them through a small learned gate. Inherited temporal features and a causal spectral filter remain part of the complete design. When retrained on KuaiRec and KuaiSAR, this design outperforms the best candidates proposed locally on those instances. It retains a 3.02% gain on KuaiRand-27K (Figure 2). The local attention branch models recent transitions alongside the existing long-range aggregation. Peer evaluations establish transfer of the complete design; their results subsequently entered the shared context of ongoing peer searches.

RL: reference-distance weighting and selective transfer.

The source-2 iteration-87 design computes each trajectory’s masked mean absolute difference between rollout-policy and reference-policy log probabilities. It centers the distance using the batch median, scales it by a robust spread, clamps it to [−6,6][-6,6], and applies a sigmoid. After advantage whitening, bounded weights amplify positive advantages for reference-like trajectories and attenuate them for distant trajectories. This modulation is reversed for negative advantages. The distance is detached, and the KL coefficient and training budget remain fixed. This reference-dependent weighting is intended to retain useful coding priors while learning from reward. The candidate regresses against its direct parent on the source (Table 24) but remains above the fixed source reference. It passes on two peers and regresses on the other two, then achieves a 6.64% larger-scale gain. The 32.35% source-local maximum instead comes from the source-2 iteration-88 quantile-threshold rollout filter; the local and larger-scale maxima are distinct discoveries. Appendix F.4 separately tests policies trained with the discovered algorithms on held-out coding tasks.

VLM: convergent discovery of global image context.

The D5-C iteration-56 design pools frozen SigLIP patch features and applies image-level FiLM to projector hidden states through a 0.1-scaled residual. It reduces full-target loss by 7.07% relative to the fixed baseline despite regressing against its direct parent on both the source and full target. D5-A had explored global image context before this candidate was published, and the D5-C record was not among the successful peer transfers shown to the D5-A iteration-83 proposal. The trace therefore supports convergent exploration of this mechanism family. D5-A iteration 83 mean-pools all image tokens, projects the summary, and adds a small gated residual to each token. At D5-A iteration 86, the broadcast intervention is applied to a different local parent; the resulting candidate uses square-root warm-up. The resulting full-target loss improves over its parent (Table 24), while source loss increases by only 0.02%. Its loss reduction relative to the 1.2071 fixed reference is 7.51%. The design supplies explicit image-level context to every patch while preserving the fixed image-token interface.

Appendix E Additional Configuration and Budget Results

E.1 Larger-scale and full-target outcomes

Figure 5 reproduces the best larger-scale outcomes from Table 2D for Track A and the best full-target outcomes from Table 4 for Track B. Each pair uses its domain’s metric and fixed reference: Track A compares PE with S after larger-scale retraining, while Track B compares PE with Direct after full-target training. All metrics are oriented so that positive relative gains indicate improvement.

E.2 Search harnesses and proposal models

This comparison tests local discovery and larger-scale transfer across harnesses and proposers. Table 25 holds the watch-time task family and EGMN starting model fixed. Panel A uses GPT-5.5 with AdaEvolve (Cemri et al., 2026), EvoX (Liu et al., 2026a), OpenEvolve (Sharma, 2025), PACEvolve (Yan et al., 2026), or AutoResearch (Karpathy, 2026). Panel B fixes AdaEvolve and varies the proposer among GPT-5.5, GPT-5.6, Claude Opus 4.8, and Claude Opus 5, all at high reasoning effort. Each S/PE pair uses the same harness and proposer. Source columns measure local discovery, while KuaiRand-27K measures larger-scale transfer of the selected designs.

E.3 LLM full-target quality, yield, and threshold sensitivity

Figure 6 summarizes the completed LLM discovery runs in Section 4.3, which use matched total GPU compute. Panel (a) reports the best full-target gain; panel (b) reports the number of candidates meeting the predefined 1% relative-improvement criterion. All executed search and evaluation stages contribute to cost under the accounting in Appendix B.5.

Sensitivity to the success threshold.

We reclassify the completed full-target results at four relative-improvement thresholds while retaining the fixed reference accuracy of 40.25% (0.4025 on the unit scale). A candidate meets threshold τ\tau when its score is at least 0.4025​(1+τ)0.4025(1+\tau). The main threshold remains the 1% criterion fixed before the reported comparisons. Table 26 shows that PE returns more successful candidates at every examined threshold. At 0.5%, Direct returns six successful candidates and PE returns 21; at 1%, 1.5%, and 2%, Direct returns none while PE returns 13, eight, and three, respectively. The best Direct gain is 0.92%, while the best PE gain is 2.48%; the quality comparison complements the threshold-dependent success counts.

Appendix F Transfer to New Datasets and Coding Tasks

F.1 Candidate selection and evaluation protocol

This appendix specifies the three transfer evaluations in Section 3.1, testing the designs returned by each complete discovery procedure beyond its discovery instances. Watch-time heads transfer to VK-LSVD; ranking designs transfer to KuaiVideo with a change from full-catalog next-item prediction to candidate-conditioned click prediction; RL modifications are evaluated on a task partition disjoint from the 423-task larger-scale selection set. The two recommendation datasets were excluded from source search, peer evaluation, and larger-scale promotion.

Candidate selection and evaluation.

Each procedure supplies candidates through its own selection rule. Each discovered intervention is evaluated without candidate-specific redesign or hyperparameter tuning, using a shared target protocol. For watch-time, PE contributes designs that passed larger-scale evaluation, and S contributes the best source candidate from each of five datasets. For ranking, PE likewise contributes designs that passed larger-scale evaluation, and S contributes the top four source candidates from each of five datasets. RL compares two successful PE candidates and the best S candidate from each of five source searches. Recommendation weights are trained from scratch on each new dataset; RL policies start from the same pretrained model and follow a fixed training protocol before evaluation on held-out coding tasks.

Target calibration and reporting.

Each recommendation target uses one baseline-calibrated configuration shared by the reference and every candidate, including the training duration. Baseline hyperparameter and training-duration selection use the released test split, which is also used for final reporting; no separate validation split is used for these selection decisions. The recommendation results therefore measure transfer to new datasets under shared target-side calibration, rather than an independent test evaluation after calibration. Candidate-specific HPO and evolutionary adaptation on these targets are disabled. The RL reference uses the fixed, unmodified training configuration without target-side HPO; the 632 coding tasks are disjoint from the larger-scale selection partition. Recommendation references and candidates are trained with three seeds; RL references and candidates undergo three independent stochastic reruns with the same nominal training seed. We report means and sample standard deviations over these three runs. These repetitions assess candidate performance rather than variability across complete discovery runs. AUC, gAUC, and pass@1 are expressed as percentages; MAE is in seconds. Means and standard deviations use two decimal places, except log loss, which uses four. All comparisons use the original precision.

Candidate-set and best-candidate summaries.

For recommendation, each candidate’s score is its three-seed mean, and candidate-set means give each evaluated candidate record equal weight. Candidate-set means measure average transfer of each procedure’s selected designs; best-candidate scores identify its strongest evaluated design by mean AUC or mean MAE. On VK-LSVD, PE and S obtain 14.54±0.0114.54\pm 0.01 s and 14.55±0.0114.55\pm 0.01 s. For each seed, we first average MAE across candidates; the reported standard deviation is then computed across these three averages. On KuaiVideo, the corresponding mean AUCs are 74.45% and 74.39%. As a weighting check, we group behaviorally equivalent implementations and aggregate their unrounded scores; equivalence is determined from implementations, not equality of rounded metrics. Counting each group once preserves the PE–S ordering: mean AUCs remain 74.45% and 74.39%, and mean MAEs remain 14.54±0.0114.54\pm 0.01 s and 14.55±0.0114.55\pm 0.01 s after rounding. The five RL source searches share the same training dataset and objective, and their discovery goal is to find the strongest algorithm for that setting. We therefore compare the best RL candidate from each method using its mean over three stochastic reruns, rather than the candidate-set mean. Table 3 summarizes the PE–S comparisons; the following subsections report the references and individual candidates.

F.2 Watch-time transfer to VK-LSVD

This evaluation tests whether a discovered distributional head remains useful on a new dataset under a common feature encoder and training protocol.

Data and shared model.

We use the HEGM-processed VK-LSVD/up0.01_ir0.01 subset of VK-LSVD (Poslavsky et al., 2026; Gulevskaia et al., 2026), retaining its chronological split and precomputed features.11 1 Raw data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/deepvk/VK-LSVD; processed release: https://github.com/rw404/HEGM. Video duration and the remaining numerical features are retained; duration buckets and categorical vocabularies are constructed from training data only. All candidates share the encoder and training settings in Table 27; only the distributional head changes.

Calibration and outcomes.

Baseline calibration monitors released-test MAE and completes 11 valid trials within a cap of 50, stopping after ten successive trials without improvement. Table 30 lists the search ranges and selected values shared by all candidates; no candidate-specific tuning follows. The shared calibrated EGMN reference has MAE 14.73±0.0214.73\pm 0.02 s. Every evaluated PE head improves its mean MAE, with paired reductions of 1.02–1.36% (Table 28). All evaluated S heads also improve over this reference. PE has lower candidate-set mean MAE (Table 3), although the strongest individual head comes from S: 14.46±0.0214.46\pm 0.02 s versus 14.53±0.0214.53\pm 0.02 s for PE. The WeChat iteration-21 head achieves 14.58±0.0314.58\pm 0.03 s and a (1.02±0.30)%(1.02\pm 0.30)\% paired MAE reduction, alongside its source-instance and KuaiRand-27K improvements. This is a concrete example of one unchanged distributional design remaining useful across datasets and training scales.

F.3 Ranking transfer to KuaiVideo click prediction

This evaluation tests sequence-model designs under both a new dataset and a different recommendation objective. A common adapter makes the starting model and selected designs compatible with candidate-conditioned click prediction.

Data and features.

We use the RecZoo KuaiVideo_x1 release with its original train/test split and ALPINE-processed visual features (Li et al., 2019).22 2 Release and feature archive: https://huggingface.co/datasets/reczoo/KuaiVideo_x1; visual features: item_visual_emb_dim64.h5. Each example contains a user, candidate item, positive and negative histories, and a binary click label; histories retain the released order and are truncated to the most recent 100 items. Categorical vocabularies use training data only, while the visual feature table remains frozen without additional normalization or dimensionality reduction. The visual feature table provides complete coverage, including the 41.81% of test rows whose candidate items map to the categorical unknown token. Users are represented by learned categorical embeddings; the released user-visual features are not used. Table 29 summarizes the data and shared adapter specifications.

Common sequence-aware CTR adapter.

The candidate item is appended as the final query token to each history. Its output states h+h^{+} and h−h^{-} summarize the positive and negative histories conditioned on that item. Because these histories lack per-item timestamps, the adapter supplies sequential positions 1,…,L+11,\ldots,L+1. Given candidate embedding ee and user embedding uu, the shared click predictor uses

p^=σ⁡(MLP⁡([h+;h−;e;h+−h−;h+⊙e;h−⊙e;u])).\hat{p}=\sigma\!\left(\operatorname{MLP}\!\left([h^{+};h^{-};e;h^{+}-h^{-};h^{+}\odot e;h^{-}\odot e;u]\right)\right).

The reference, S candidates, and PE candidates use this identical adapter and differ only in the discovered sequence-model design.

Calibration and final training.

Baseline calibration uses 50 serial Optuna TPE trials, permitting two to five epochs with early-stopping patience two. Hyperparameters and the training duration are selected using released-test AUC. The selected configuration in Table 30 is shared by all candidates, which train for exactly four epochs and are evaluated once afterward. Each candidate is trained under three seeds; AUC is the primary metric, with sample-weighted user gAUC and binary log loss as auxiliary metrics.

Transfer outcome.

The best PE candidate, discovered on KuaiRand-Pure, adds a gated spectral causal long-filter channel. Its mean AUC exceeds that of the best S design from KuaiRand-1K by 0.04 percentage points computed from unrounded means, with improvements in both auxiliary metrics (Table 31). Every evaluated PE design exceeds the shared calibrated reference in mean AUC, with increases of approximately 0.04–0.07 percentage points computed before rounding (Table 32). Eight evaluated S candidates exceed the reference mean (Table 33). At the candidate-set level, mean AUC is 74.45% for PE and 74.39% for S. These results support design transfer under a common CTR adapter and shared target-side calibration; the small PE–S differences are descriptive comparisons of three-seed means.

F.4 RL transfer to a disjoint LiveCodeBench partition

This evaluation tests policies trained with the discovered RL algorithms on held-out coding tasks under a fixed training protocol.

Task partition and training.

The 1,055 LiveCodeBench tasks comprise 423 larger-scale selection tasks and 632 held-out tasks with disjoint IDs, both scored using private tests. All methods use Qwen2.5-Coder-3B-Instruct, the same larger-scale configuration, and 50 GRPO rollout steps. Candidates change the GRPO loss and/or rollout filtering; held-out coding tasks are used only to evaluate the trained policies. Each candidate is freshly trained and evaluated in three stochastic reruns with the same nominal training seed.

Best-candidate comparison.

PE obtains mean pass@1 of (23.10±0.32)%(23.10\pm 0.32)\%, compared with (22.94±0.16)%(22.94\pm 0.16)\% for S (Table 3). The unmodified reference reaches (23.26±0.42)%(23.26\pm 0.42)\% pass@1. The reference, best PE candidate, and best S candidate solve 147, 146, and 145 tasks on average, respectively (Table 34). Thus PE exceeds S by one solved task on average, while neither candidate exceeds the reference mean. These are descriptive comparisons across three stochastic reruns.

Appendix G Limitations and Future Directions

RMD-Bench covers five task families, with compatible intervention interfaces within each family. The transfer results apply to the architectures, training protocols, and evaluation settings studied here; extending PE to less compatible tasks may require additional interface design. Track A evaluates design generalization, whereas Track B targets improvement on a specified expensive workload.

The source-level comparison tests shared experimental feedback; larger-scale and full-target results evaluate the complete discovery procedures. Given the cost of full runs, further independent searches would help characterize variability in discovered designs and final performance (Appendix B.5). Future work can also examine alternative exchange and promotion policies and extend the benchmark to additional task families.
